title: Scientific diasporas: a new approach to the brain drain
authors: Jean-Baptiste Meyer, Mercy Brown
venue: UNESCO MOST Discussion Paper Series No. 41 (SHS.99/WS/12), prepared for the World Conference on Science, UNESCO-ICSU, Budapest, 26 June-1 July 1999
research_question: How are countries organizing their expatriate scientists and engineers into networks for development at home, and what lessons follow?
data: Inventory or review of existing science and technology diaspora networks. Later work cites it as an early list of such networks (record-level; full text not read).
methods: Descriptive survey and policy analysis.
findings: Record/introduction-level only. Although national experiences differ, the diaspora initiatives share the goal of systematically using expatriate experts, scientists and engineers for development at home. The authors draw early lessons and policy implications for more efficient use of S&T diasporas. Later studies use it as a baseline list of science diaspora networks. The specific counts and findings were not verified.
relevance_to_project: The founding statement of the scientific diaspora option, useful for framing SSA scientific diasporas as policy objects that differ from total migrant stocks.
verification_source: No DOI exists (grey literature). Bibliographic details come from the UNESDOC record (ark:/48223/pf0000116330) returned by WebSearch.

title: Network Approach versus Brain Drain: Lessons from the Diaspora
authors: Jean-Baptiste Meyer
research_question: Can networks of highly skilled expatriates turn the brain drain into a brain gain for origin countries?
data: Case studies of intellectual and scientific diaspora networks (abstract-level).
methods: Conceptual analysis using a connectionist or network approach, drawing on case-study evidence.
findings: Abstract-level. Highly skilled expatriate networks that connect diaspora members to their origin countries can turn brain drain into brain gain. Proposes an expanded concept of the network that includes actors and intermediaries, not only kinship or co-national ties.
relevance_to_project: Defines the diaspora knowledge network as an organized, selective subset of the diaspora, separate from the migrant population as a whole. This supports the hypothesis that knowledge partners will not simply mirror migrant destinations.
verification_source: WebSearch results: IRD documentation catalogue (fdi:010071777) and HAL deposit (ird-01730582) give International Migration 39(5) 91-110 with DOI 10.1111/1468-2435.00173.

title: Inventor migration and knowledge flows: A two-way communication channel?
authors: Ernest Miguelez, Claudia Noumedem Temgoua
research_question: Does inventor migration raise knowledge flows in both directions, back to home countries and into host countries?
data: Country-pair data for 1990-2010 on inventor migration and international patent citations (abstract-level).
methods: Country-pair gravity model of cross-country patent citations, with instrumental variables and country-pair fixed effects.
findings: Abstract-level. Inventor migration robustly increases knowledge flows to home countries under IV and pair fixed effects. The effect on flows into host countries does not hold up. The effects matter mainly when sending countries are developing countries and for knowledge diffusion within multinationals.
relevance_to_project: Shows that the knowledge payoff of migration is directional and concentrated in developing origins, which is relevant to SSA. Supports keeping direction (origin to destination) in the mobility and migrant-stock layers even though co-authorship is undirected, and testing for asymmetry in residuals.
verification_source: WebSearch results: University of Barcelona repository (hdl 2445/219164) and HAL (hal-03097427) give Research Policy 49(9) article 103914 with DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2019.103914.

title: Inventor Diasporas and the Internationalization of Technology
authors: Ernest Miguélez
research_question: Do diasporas of highly skilled (inventor) migrants increase cross-country inventive collaboration (co-patenting) and R&D offshoring between their host and origin countries?
data: PCT patent applications. Inventors with a migrant background are used as a proxy for the skilled diaspora in each country pair.
methods: Gravity models of bilateral international co-patenting (inventor-inventor co-inventorship and applicant-inventor links). Earlier versions are GREThA WP 2014-12 and World Bank Policy Research WP 7619.
findings: Abstract-level: inventor diasporas are strongly and robustly associated with international co-patenting, and the effect shrinks as interactions become more formal (stronger for inventor-inventor co-inventorship than for applicant-inventor offshoring). The Chinese and Indian diasporas do not drive the results. The working-paper version reports that a 10% larger inventor diaspora is associated with 1.5-2.2% more international patent collaborations (not confirmed in the published version).
relevance_to_project: The methodological template for including a skilled-diaspora stock in a PPML gravity model of bilateral knowledge collaboration. It is the patent analogue of our co-authorship model, and its contrast between skilled diaspora and general migration parallels our comparison of scholarly mobility with UN DESA migrant stocks.
verification_source: WebSearch: the summary of the IDEAS/EconPapers record (RePEc:oup:wbecrv:v:32:y:2018:i:1:p:41-63) gives DOI 10.1093/wber/lhw013 with the matching title. The DOI was not shown in a URL, and the Crossref API was blocked.

title: Studying scientific migration in Scopus
authors: Henk F. Moed; M'hamed Aisati; Andrew Plume
research_question: Can Scopus author profiles and affiliation linking be used to measure international scientific migration, and how do migration patterns relate to international co-authorship?
data: Scopus author-affiliation histories for five countries (Germany, Italy, Netherlands, UK, USA), 1999-2010.
methods: Bibliometric tracking of author affiliation changes, compared with co-authorship patterns between the same countries.
findings: Abstract-level: language similarity between countries is a more important factor in international migration than in international co-authorship. Example balances are given (the Netherlands had a positive migration balance with the UK and a negative one with Germany). A secondary search summary attributes to the paper the result that having international co-authors increases the probability of international movement (not confirmed in full text).
relevance_to_project: Early direct evidence that migration and co-authorship respond differently to the same dyadic factors (language), which supports treating them as distinct layers and expecting misalignment. Its scholarly-migration measure is the methodological ancestor of the Akbaritabar et al. (2024) flows we use.
verification_source: WebSearch: the IDEAS/RePEc URL encodes 10.1007/s11192-012-0783-9 with the matching title, and an api.crossref.org/works/10.1007/S11192-012-0783-9 link and an Unpaywall link appeared in the results. The Crossref API itself was not fetchable.

title: International collaboration in scientific publishing: the case of West Africa (2001-2010)
authors: Eustache Mêgnigbêto
research_question: Who are West African countries' co-authorship partners, and how much do they collaborate with each other compared with African and non-African countries?
data: Web of Science publications with at least one author affiliated in any of the 15 West African countries, 2001-2010.
methods: Descriptive bibliometric co-authorship partner analysis.
findings: Abstract-level only. The main African partners are South Africa, Cameroon, Kenya and Tanzania. The main non-African partners are France, the USA and the UK, which together account for over 63% of papers with a non-West-African address. West African countries collaborate less with each other and with other African and developing countries than with developed countries.
relevance_to_project: Gives expected collaboration-partner profiles for Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal (France/US/UK dominance and weak intra-regional ties) to compare with their UN DESA migrant-destination profiles, which are often more regional (ECOWAS corridors). This is a likely source of misalignment.
verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding 10.1007/s11192-013-0963-2 (Scientometrics v96 i3), the University of Antwerp repository record, and a doi.org/10.1007/S11192-013-0963-2 result.

title: Knowledge production through collaborative research in sub-Saharan Africa: how much do countries contribute to each other's knowledge output and citation impact?
authors: Omwoyo Bosire Onyancha; Jan Resenga Maluleka
research_question: How much do sub-Saharan African countries co-produce knowledge with each other, compared with partners outside the region, and what is the citation impact?
data: Publications and citations of sub-Saharan African countries (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
methods: Co-authorship (co-production) and citation counts by country pair.
findings: Abstract-level only. Collaboration among sub-Saharan African countries is minimal and contributes only a small share compared with collaboration with foreign partners. The authors recommend student and staff exchange, regional conferences and research networks.
relevance_to_project: Documents weak intra-SSA co-authorship. Since a large share of SSA migrant stock stays within the region (e.g., Somalia to Kenya/Ethiopia, Uganda to Kenya), this predicts a structural gap between the migration layer and the knowledge layer for the focus origins.
verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc URL encoding 10.1007/s11192-010-0330-5 (Scientometrics v87 i2) and the Unpaywall/Unisa repository records for the same DOI.

title: Analyzing scientific mobility and collaboration in the Middle East and North Africa
authors: Jamal El Ouahi; Nicolás Robinson-García; Rodrigo Costas
research_question: How do scientific mobility and international collaboration networks of MENA countries compare in structure and in partner affinity?
data: Bibliometric publication and affiliation data for MENA countries, 2008-2017. A dataset is archived on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.5155979). The arXiv preprint is 2009.07815.
methods: Country-level mobility and co-authorship networks, degree and affinity indicators, and comparison of the two layers.
findings: Abstract-level from search snippets: international co-authorship is more frequent than international mobility. The mobility network is thinner than the collaboration network in terms of affinity between countries. The hubs differ: Saudi Arabia has the highest degree in mobility, while Turkey has the highest in collaboration.
relevance_to_project: A regional precedent (including North Africa) for comparing the partner structure of a mobility layer with a collaboration layer and finding non-alignment, methodologically parallel to our per-origin alignment and topology comparison. Like the other CWTS/Sugimoto studies, it uses only scholarly mobility and no general migrant stocks.

The DOI was not shown in a URL, and Crossref could not be queried because api.crossref.org is blocked.

title: Migrant Networks and Trade: The Vietnamese Boat People as a Natural Experiment
authors: Christopher Parsons, Pierre-Louis Vezina
research_question: Do migrant networks causally increase trade with their origin country?
data: Distribution of Vietnamese refugees across US states and US state-level exports to Vietnam after the trade embargo was lifted in 1994 (abstract-level). Working paper: IZA DP 10112.
methods: Natural experiment: refugee dispersal across US states during a trade embargo, followed by embargo removal.
findings: Abstract-level. After trade restrictions were lifted in 1994, US exports to Vietnam grew most in states with larger Vietnamese populations, which themselves resulted from larger refugee inflows about 20 years earlier.
relevance_to_project: A causal benchmark showing that refugee-origin diasporas can create economic ties. That bears on whether refugee-driven stocks such as the Somali and Ethiopian diasporas translate into scientific ties, and it provides an identification template.

title: Co-evolution of international scientific mobility and international collaboration: a Scopus-based analysis
authors: Ruimin Pei, Langqiu Li, Yiying Yang, Quan Zhou
research_question: How have international scientific mobility networks and international collaboration networks co-evolved, and how closely aligned are they across countries?
data: Scopus-derived country-level mobility and collaboration networks over a long period; one summary gives the start year as 1788, possibly a typo, ending in 2020.
methods: Network analysis of mobility (talent flow) and collaboration networks over time and their alignment. QAP correlation is not confirmed from what I saw.
findings: Abstract-level (fragments). The global flow and collaboration networks are increasingly interconnected. There is a 'Matthew effect': a few dominant countries and many minor participants. Advanced countries show closer alignment between their collaboration and mobility networks than lagging countries. The paper offers policy suggestions on mobility and engaging peripheral countries.
relevance_to_project: Direct precedent for comparing the mobility and collaboration layers. Its finding of weaker alignment for lagging countries matches the project's hypothesis for Sub-Saharan origins. It does not appear to include general migrant stocks or origin-specific distributional divergence with nulls.

title: Multiscale impact of researcher mobility
authors: Alexander M. Petersen
venue: Journal of the Royal Society Interface 15(146), 20180580
research_question: What are the effects of cross-border researcher mobility on citation impact, topic diversity, collaboration and international integration?
data: American Physical Society journals 1980-2009; 26,170 disambiguated prominent researcher profiles (dataset on Dryad).
methods: Matching mobile researchers to similar non-mobile researchers on pre-move profile attributes, followed by a 10-year window around each move. Outcomes cover individual impact, co-author diversity, collaboration network churn and international integration, across three time periods.
findings: Abstract and summary level. Mobile researchers gain up to a 17% citation advantage, attributed to a simultaneous increase in co-author diversity. Researchers completely curtail prior collaborations with their source country in 11% of cross-border moves. Effects appear across scales, from careers to collaboration network churn to international integration, and virtual channels do not appear to replace physical mobility.
relevance_to_project: One of the few studies that directly links a move to later co-authorship. Most movers keep ties to the origin country (only 11% fully curtail them), so the mobility layer should predict origin-destination co-authorship in both directions, while collaboration networks also churn after moves. It covers physics only, mostly in high-income systems.
verification_source: WebSearch results included PMC6170771 with title 'Multiscale impact of researcher mobility'; the search summary gave J R Soc Interface 15(146):20180580, DOI 10.1098/rsif.2018.0580, sole author A. M. Petersen. My query did not contain the DOI.

title: Research emphasis and collaboration in Africa
authors: Anastassios Pouris; Yuh-Shan Ho
research_question: Which disciplines does African research emphasize, and what are African collaboration patterns at country and continental level?
data: African publications (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
methods: Co-authorship analysis at country and continental level, plus disciplinary profiling.
findings: Abstract-level only. Collaboration rates in Africa are substantially higher than in the rest of the world. Research emphasis leans toward medical and natural-resource disciplines rather than fields supporting knowledge-based economies.
relevance_to_project: The very high international co-authorship share of African output means OpenAlex co-authorship edges for focus origins are dense and partner-heavy. This matters for null-model design and for full versus fractional counting. The medical emphasis suggests field-specific partner structures (e.g., global health funders).

title: The many faces of mobility: Using bibliometric data to measure the movement of scientists
authors: Nicolas Robinson-Garcia, Cassidy R. Sugimoto, Dakota Murray, Alfredo Yegros-Yegros, Vincent Lariviere, Rodrigo Costas
research_question: How can publication affiliation data be used to build a typology and indicators of scientific mobility?
data: About 16 million authors in Web of Science, 2008-2015 (arXiv preprint 1803.03449).
methods: A typology of mobility based on affiliation sequences. 'Migrants' break ties with their origin country. 'Travelers' add foreign affiliations while keeping origin ties, and are split into directional and non-directional. Country-level incoming and outgoing classifications are also built.
findings: Abstract-level. About 3.7% of authors were mobile. Travelers make up most mobile scholars (72.7% per one summary), but migrants have higher scientific impact; impact ranks migrants first, then directional travelers, non-directional travelers and non-mobile researchers.
relevance_to_project: Key for interpreting the Akbaritabar flows. Multiple and concurrent affiliations ('travelers') sit on the boundary between mobility and collaboration. A traveler with a home affiliation and a foreign affiliation produces co-authorship-like cross-country links, so the scholarly mobility layer and the co-authorship layer are not independent. The paper's directional typology supports treating origin-to-destination direction explicitly rather than symmetrising.
verification_source: EconPapers RePEc record (eee:infome v13 i1 p50-63) surfaced via WebSearch; the search summary reported DOI 10.1016/J.JOI.2018.11.002 with this title. arXiv 1803.03449 also listed with the same title.

title: From Brain Drain to Brain Circulation: Transnational Communities and Regional Upgrading in India and China
authors: AnnaLee Saxenian
research_question: How are Indian and Chinese immigrant engineers and entrepreneurs in Silicon Valley influencing economic development in their home regions?
data: Qualitative evidence on transnational technical communities, returnees and cross-border venture capital (abstract-level; author's pre-print hosted at Berkeley).
methods: Comparative qualitative and case-study analysis.
findings: Abstract-level. Transnational communities of Indian and Chinese skilled migrants, including returnees, link Silicon Valley with their home regions and help upgrade them technologically. This shifts the pattern from one-way brain drain to two-way brain circulation.
relevance_to_project: The source of the brain circulation concept. It suggests that the relevant knowledge layer is circulation (mobility and return), not static stocks. That supports treating Akbaritabar mobility flows as distinct from UN DESA stocks.
verification_source: A WebSearch for the article returned a doi.org/10.1007/BF02686293 result together with the Berkeley iSchool publication record (SCID 40(2), 2005). Springer and Crossref pages were not directly readable, so this is moderately strong confirmation.

title: Migrant scientists and international networks
authors: Giuseppe Scellato; Chiara Franzoni; Paula Stephan
research_question: Do foreign-born (migrant) scientists have more international research collaborations than non-migrants and returnees, and do they keep collaborating with their country of origin?
data: GlobSci survey (2011) of scientists working in 16 countries, comparing foreign-born, native non-mobile, and returnee scientists. An earlier version is NBER WP 18613 (2012), 'Mobile Scientists and International Networks'.
methods: Survey-based econometric comparison of collaboration patterns by migration status and by where the PhD was obtained.
findings: Abstract-level: migrants are more likely to collaborate internationally, mainly those who did their PhD abroad and came to the destination for a postdoc or a job. A sizeable share of the foreign-born collaborate with researchers in their country of origin (a 'diaspora effect'). Migrants from a relatively stronger science base have superior networks to those from a weaker one.
relevance_to_project: Individual-level micro-foundation for a migrant-to-origin co-authorship link. The result that network benefits depend on the origin's science base implies that for weak-science-base origins (many SSA focus countries) migrant destinations may not translate into collaboration partners, which is the mismatch hypothesis. Useful for interpreting PPML coefficients on migrant stocks by origin capacity.
verification_source: WebSearch results showing the iris.polito.it record ('RESEARCH POLICY 44:1 (2015), pp. 108-120 [10.1016/j.respol.2014.07.014]') and the RePEc record RePEc:eee:respol:v:44:y:2015:i:1:p:108-120. A direct Crossref API check was blocked by the network (api.crossref.org not allowlisted).

title: Extracting the multiscale backbone of complex weighted networks
authors: M. Ángeles Serrano, Marián Boguñá, Alessandro Vespignani
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(16):6483-6488
research_question: How can the relevant backbone of a large, heterogeneous weighted network be extracted without a global weight threshold that discards small-scale but locally important links?
data: Real-world weighted networks, including a food web (abstract-level; full list not checked).
methods: Disparity filter: under a local null model, each node's strength is spread uniformly at random over its edges. An edge is kept if its normalized weight is significantly larger than this null at significance level alpha, for at least one endpoint. Compared with global thresholding and other backbone methods.
findings: Abstract-level: the filter keeps locally significant edges at all scales of the weight distribution, does not penalize small-scale interactions, and reportedly beats global thresholding at keeping structure while shrinking the network.
relevance_to_project: Useful for building comparable backbones of the migration, mobility and co-authorship layers. Weights differ by orders of magnitude between South Africa/Nigeria and Somalia/Rwanda, so a local, strength-normalized filter avoids backbones that only show large origins. Alpha sensitivity should be reported.
verification_source: WebSearch results (Crossref blocked): Scilit record lists https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0808904106 (query without the DOI string returned it); ISI Foundation-hosted PDF 'pnas-2009-serrano-6483-8'; arXiv 0904.2389.

title: The relation between global migration and trade networks
authors: Paolo Sgrignoli, Rodolfo Metulini, Stefano Schiavo, Massimo Riccaboni
venue: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications 417:245-260
research_question: Does global migration increase bilateral trade, and for which product categories?
data: Global bilateral migration and trade networks, including product-level trade (abstract-level). Preprint: arXiv:1310.3716; IMT Lucca EIC WP 6/2013.
methods: A hypergeometric network filter isolates links where both migration and trade exceed their expected values given node totals, followed by spatial-econometric estimation.
findings: Abstract-level. Migration increases trade between countries, and the authors identify product categories where the effect is strongest.
relevance_to_project: The hypergeometric filter is a margin-preserving null that applies directly to the planned observed-versus-expected residual analysis. It can identify country pairs over-represented in both the migration layer and the co-authorship layer.
verification_source: WebSearch results: EconPapers (RePEc:eee:phsmap:v:417:y:2015:i:c:p:245-260) and the arXiv 1310.3716 listing give Physica A 417 245-260 with DOI 10.1016/j.physa.2014.09.037.

title: The log of gravity
authors: J. M. C. Santos Silva, Silvana Tenreyro
research_question: Are elasticities from log-linearized gravity equations estimated by OLS consistent, and if not, what estimator should be used?
data: Bilateral trade data, with an Anderson-van Wincoop gravity specification as the application (abstract-level).
methods: Shows analytically (via Jensen's inequality) that under heteroskedasticity OLS on log-linearized models is inconsistent for the elasticities, and proposes the Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML) estimator on levels.
findings: Abstract-level: log-linearized OLS gives biased elasticities under heteroskedasticity. In the application, OLS overstates the role of geographic distance, with the log-linear distance elasticity almost twice the PPML (levels) estimate.
relevance_to_project: The foundational justification for estimating the co-authorship gravity model by PPML on counts, not OLS on log(1+y). This matters given the many zero or small co-authorship counts and heteroskedastic errors for SSA dyads.
verification_source: WebSearch results (Crossref blocked): EconPapers RePEc:tpr:restat:v:88:y:2006:i:4:p:641-658; author PDF named rest.88.4.641.pdf; LSE eprints 2510 record.

title: Analytical maximum-likelihood method to detect patterns in real networks
authors: Tiziano Squartini, Diego Garlaschelli
research_question: How can null-model expectations for network properties be obtained analytically and without bias, instead of by sampling randomized networks?
data: Real binary and weighted networks (abstract-level; applications include degree correlations and clustering in binary undirected networks).
methods: Maximum-entropy ensembles constrained on chosen local properties (degrees, strengths), with parameters fitted by maximum likelihood. Gives analytical expectations and standard deviations for topological properties in binary/weighted and directed/undirected networks.
findings: Abstract-level: gives exact expectations and standard deviations without generating randomized graphs. The authors argue that common quantities such as modularity rest on incorrect null expressions and supply corrected ones.
relevance_to_project: The analytical basis for degree- and strength-preserving nulls (for example a weighted configuration model) for each layer. Observed edge overlap, reciprocity, clustering and per-origin partner distributions can then be expressed as z-scores, not compared raw across layers of different density.
verification_source: WebSearch results (Crossref blocked): the search returned DOI 10.1088/1367-2630/13/8/083001 although the query did not contain it; arXiv 1103.0701; IMT Lucca IRIS record; EconPapers LEM WP 2011/07 (earlier title 'Exact maximum-likelihood method...').

title: Scientists have most impact when they're free to move
authors: Cassidy R. Sugimoto, Nicolas Robinson-Garcia, Dakota S. Murray, Alfredo Yegros-Yegros, Rodrigo Costas, Vincent Lariviere
research_question: How common is international researcher mobility, and how is mobility associated with citation impact across countries and regions?
data: Web of Science papers 2008-2015: about 14 million papers and about 16 million authors, with mobility inferred from changes in country of affiliation.
methods: Authors are classified as non-mobile or mobile depending on whether their affiliation country changed during the window. Citation impact is compared between mobile and non-mobile authors by country and region.
findings: From secondary and press summaries; I did not see the full text. About 96% of authors were non-mobile and about 4% mobile. Mobile scholars had about 40% higher citation rates on average than non-mobile ones, with the advantage varying by region (about 10.8% for North Americans). The authors argue that restricting circulation harms science. Commentators note the result is correlational, since selection into mobility is not ruled out.
relevance_to_project: This is the founding paper of the WoS-based mobility indicator programme and the companion to Wagner & Jonkers. It shows that bibliometric mobility covers a small, selective share of researchers, which helps explain why the scholarly mobility layer can diverge from general migrant stocks. It does not model co-authorship partner distributions.
verification_source: WebSearch results showed a nature.com PDF path ending '550029a.pdf' and institutional listings (INGENIO-UPV, CIRST) with this title and author list; the search summary gave DOI 10.1038/550029a and Nature 550(7674):29-31. Crossref was not reachable.

title: Highly skilled migration and the internationalization of knowledge
authors: Claudia Noumedem Temgoua
venue: Cahiers du GREThA (Université de Bordeaux) Working Paper n° 2018-16
research_question: Do Chinese and Indian highly skilled diasporas foster international knowledge networks (co-authorship and co-inventorship) among OECD destination countries?
data: OECD destination-country pairs, with bilateral co-authorship (publications) and co-inventorship (patents) and highly skilled diaspora stocks by origin (China, India; also Vietnam, Pakistan, Iran).
methods: Gravity model at the country-pair level. The search summary of the working paper text describes PPML estimation with co-authorship and co-inventorship as dependent variables, controlling for other migration variables.
findings: Abstract-level: OECD country pairs hosting sizeable portions of the Indian or Chinese highly skilled diaspora collaborate more on publications and patents, after controlling for other migration variables. Smaller diasporas (Vietnam, Pakistan, Iran) produce similar effects on co-authorship and co-inventorship.
relevance_to_project: The closest precedent found for component (b): a PPML gravity model of bilateral co-authorship that separates a skilled-diaspora variable from other migration controls. Its dyads are destination-destination pairs linked by a shared third-country diaspora, whereas ours are origin-destination pairs with SSA origins, and it does not use bibliometric scholarly mobility. Journal publication status is unknown.
verification_source: No DOI exists or none was found. Title, author, series and number were seen in WebSearch results (EconPapers RePEc:grt:wpegrt:2018-16 and the cahiersdugretha.u-bordeaux.fr PDF). A direct fetch of the GREThA page was blocked by the network.

title: Africa's contribution to the worldwide research literature: New analytical perspectives, trends, and performance indicators
authors: Robert J. W. Tijssen
research_question: How large is Africa's research output and how has it changed (1980-2004) in international and national/regional journals, and what do co-publication patterns show?
data: Research publications by Africa-based authors, 1980-2004, in international journals (Web of Science) and in national and regional journals.
methods: Descriptive scientometric trend and performance indicators, including international co-publication shares.
findings: Abstract-level only. Africa's share of worldwide science in international journals declined steadily over the period, while international co-publication grew considerably.
relevance_to_project: Historical baseline showing African science becoming more internationally co-authored while its global share shrank. This makes partner choice (former colonial powers, the US, South Africa) central to comparing collaboration partners with migrant destinations.
verification_source: WebSearch results: IDEAS/RePEc page whose URL encodes 10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3 (Scientometrics v71 i2, pp. 303-327) and a link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11192-007-1658-3 result. An exact-DOI-string search found no direct hit at first, but the IDEAS and Springer URLs confirm it.

title: Talent goes to global cities: The world network of scientists' mobility
authors: Luca Verginer, Massimo Riccaboni
research_question: How is the world network of scientists' mobility structured at city level, and do global cities attract and retain the most productive scientists?
data: Disambiguated author publication histories at city level. The full-text PDF describes 3.7 million authors and 7,159 cities; another summary says about 2 million researchers and more than 2,000 cities over a decade. The source database is not confirmed from what I saw.
methods: Construction of a city-level mobility network and analysis of the centrality of global cities, plus the productivity of scientists they attract and retain.
findings: Abstract and full-text fragments. Global cities attract and retain the most productive scientists, benefiting from their central position in the international mobility network by attracting and retaining prolific scientists early in their careers.
relevance_to_project: Shows that scholarly mobility concentrates on a few hubs, which matters for the multilayer topology comparison and for strength-preserving nulls, since hub concentration may differ from the more diffuse geography of general migrant stocks. City-level work also warns that country aggregation hides within-country concentration.
verification_source: WebSearch results showed the ETH research-collection record and the IDEAS record (eee/respol v50y2021i1 s004873332030202x) with this title; the search summary gave DOI 10.1016/j.respol.2020.104127 and Research Policy 50(1) 104127. The PDF filename (S004873332030202X) matches the PII.

title: Network structure, self-organization, and the growth of international collaboration in science
authors: Caroline S. Wagner; Loet Leydesdorff
research_question: Why has international co-authorship grown so fast, and is the growth better explained by network self-organization (preferential attachment) than by national policy or funding?
data: International co-authorship links between countries, built from bibliometric (ISI/Web of Science) records. Abstract-level only; the exact years were not checked.
methods: Network analysis of the country co-authorship network, including degree distributions and tests of preferential attachment / self-organization.
findings: Abstract-level only. The authors describe international collaboration as a self-organizing network whose growth follows network dynamics (preferential attachment to well-connected countries) more than national or institutional incentives.
relevance_to_project: This is the standard framing of the country-level co-authorship layer as a self-organizing network. It explains why the knowledge layer may follow its own core-periphery logic rather than the migration layer, which motivates the degree/strength-preserving null models and the multilayer topology comparison.
verification_source: WebSearch results: Scilit record (scilit.net) giving https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2005.08.002 with Research Policy 34(10):1608-1618, and the EconPapers RePEc handle for the same volume, issue and pages.

title: The continuing growth of global cooperation networks in research: A conundrum for national governments
authors: Caroline S. Wagner; Han Woo Park; Loet Leydesdorff
research_question: How has the global network of international co-authorship evolved, and what does its growth mean for national science policy?
data: Internationally co-authored publications between countries over about two decades (bibliometric database). Abstract-level only.
methods: Network analysis of country co-authorship networks over time.
findings: Abstract-level only. The share of internationally co-authored papers has more than doubled in 20 years and accounts for the output growth of advanced countries. The network acts as a new organization alongside national systems. Emerging countries, especially China, are participating more. International collaboration does not appear to threaten national science and may improve its quality.
relevance_to_project: Background on the growth and densification of the co-authorship layer. Its claim that the network is a supranational structure supports testing whether co-authorship partners diverge from migration corridors.
verification_source: WebSearch results: PubMed Central record PMC4510583 and DOAJ/library catalogue records reporting DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0131816, published 21 July 2015.

title: Open countries have strong science
authors: Caroline S. Wagner, Koen Jonkers
research_question: Is a country's openness to international engagement, through collaboration and researcher mobility, associated with the impact of its science?
data: Country-level indicators for a set of leading scientific countries: share of internationally co-authored papers and researcher mobility (inflows and outflows), plus citation impact.
methods: Construction of an openness index combining international collaboration and mobility, and correlation of openness with citation impact. A 2018 follow-up ('Openness and Impact of Leading Scientific Countries', arXiv 1810.07812) extends it.
findings: From secondary sources and the follow-up. There is a clear correlation between a nation's scientific influence and its links with foreign researchers: more open countries produce higher-impact science. The follow-up warns that the correlation does not imply all countries have equal potential to open up, and that results do not extend to unanalysed countries.
relevance_to_project: Treats collaboration and mobility as two parts of one openness construct, a framing the project questions. It covers only leading countries, not Sub-Saharan Africa, so its pooling of mobility and collaboration may not hold for peripheral origins.
verification_source: WebSearch result list showed the IDEAS record URL nat/nature v550y2017i7674 d10.1038_550032a; the search summary gave the title 'Open countries have strong science', Nature 550(7674):32-33.

title: Field-normalized citation impact indicators and the choice of an appropriate counting method
authors: Ludo Waltman; Nees Jan van Eck
research_question: Which counting method (full or fractional, and which fractional variant) gives properly field-normalized indicators for countries and organizations?
data: Web of Science publications and citations (CWTS); also arXiv:1501.04431. Abstract-level only.
methods: Theoretical argument plus empirical comparison of full counting and several fractional counting variants.
findings: Abstract-level only. Full counting does not give properly field-normalized results, while fractional counting does. The authors recommend fractional counting for field-normalized studies, especially at country and organization level.
relevance_to_project: Shapes how the OpenAlex co-authorship edges are weighted: full counts of papers per dyad versus fractional/author-share weights. The choice changes gravity estimates and partner distributions, especially for small African systems with very high international co-authorship shares. Both should be run as a robustness check.
verification_source: WebSearch results: EconPapers RePEc record (J. Informetrics 9(4):872-894) giving DOI 10.1016/j.joi.2015.08.001, and the arXiv preprint 1501.04431.

title: Return migration of German-affiliated researchers: analyzing departure and return by gender, cohort, and discipline using Scopus bibliometric data 1996-2020
authors: Xinyi Zhao, Samin Aref, Emilio Zagheni, Guy Stecklov
research_question: Who among researchers who leave Germany returns, and how does return vary by gender, cohort, discipline, destination and continued collaboration with German-affiliated researchers?
data: Scopus: about 8 million publications by about 1.1 million researchers who published at least once with a German affiliation, 1996-2020 (arXiv 2110.08340).
methods: Bibliometric identification of departure and return events from affiliation histories, with descriptive cohort analysis and models of return propensity including collaboration ties to Germany while abroad.
findings: Abstract-level. Return migration declines slightly in more recent cohorts, which for most disciplines coincides with fewer German collaboration ties. Women who leave are less likely than men to return. Keeping collaborations with German-affiliated researchers while abroad has a moderate positive association with return. Per a Population Europe digest, those who moved to high R&D-spending countries were less likely to return.
relevance_to_project: Evidence that collaboration ties with the origin persist after emigration and predict return, so knowledge links run in both directions along migration corridors. It supports modelling both directions of mobility and treating origin-destination co-authorship as partly a diaspora tie. It is a single-origin case in a high-income country.
verification_source: WebSearch results (MPIDR journal-article page, arXiv 2110.08340, Population Europe) showed this title; the search summary gave Scientometrics 127(12):7707-7729 and DOI 10.1007/s11192-022-04351-4. My query did not contain the DOI.

title: Where on Earth is Everybody? The Evolution of Global Bilateral Migration 1960-2000
authors: Çağlar Özden, Christopher R. Parsons, Maurice Schiff, Terrie L. Walmsley
research_question: What do complete global bilateral migrant-stock matrices look like for 1960-2000, and how has global migration evolved?
data: More than 1,000 census and population-register records, used to build bilateral migrant-stock matrices for 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990 and 2000, disaggregated by gender, mainly on a foreign-born definition.
methods: Harmonization of census and register data, with imputation and estimation to fill missing bilateral cells and reconcile definitions.
findings: Abstract-level: the global migrant stock rose from 92 million (1960) to 165 million (2000). Migration between developing countries was about half of all international migration in 2000, and developing-to-developed migration was the fastest-growing component. The US hosted about one fifth of the world's migrants.
relevance_to_project: The methodological precursor of current bilateral stock data (the UN DESA estimates build on similar census-based harmonization). It documents that bilateral stocks are destination-census-based and partly imputed, which matters for SSA origins with large intra-African (south-south) migration that knowledge-network layers may not reflect.
